title: What are Kubernetes QoS classes (Guaranteed = requests==limits, Burstable = requests<limits, BestEffort = none), how do they affect which pods are OOM-killed first under node memory pressure, and why is `emptyDir` volume data lost when a pod is restarted/rescheduled (it's tied to the pod lifecycle)?
shortTitle: Kubernetes QoS Classes, OOM Eviction Order, and Why emptyDir Data Is Lost

s1_definition.profdef: Kubernetes assigns each Pod a Quality of Service class based on its resource requests and limits. Guaranteed means every container sets requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory. Burstable means at least one container sets a request but not equal-limits for all resources. BestEffort means no requests or limits at all. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts in the order BestEffort first, then Burstable that exceed their requests, and Guaranteed last, and the OOM killer uses a correlated oom_score so BestEffort processes are killed before Guaranteed ones. An emptyDir volume shares the Pod's lifecycle, so its data is created when the Pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the Pod is removed or rescheduled, which is why its contents do not survive a reschedule.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, when the branch runs short of space, management decides who gets moved out first. BestEffort tellers made no reservation, so they are moved first. Burstable tellers reserved a small desk but spread onto extra space, so they are moved next if they overflowed their reservation. Guaranteed tellers reserved exactly the space they use, so they are protected and moved last. An emptyDir is a scratch notepad clipped to the teller's badge; the moment that teller leaves the building the notepad is thrown away, so nothing written on it survives their departure.
s1_definition.oneliner: Guaranteed Pods survive longest and BestEffort die first under memory pressure, and emptyDir is scratch space tied to the Pod, so it vanishes on restart or reschedule.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kubernetes assigns each Pod a Quality of Service class based on its resource requests and limits. Guaranteed means every container sets requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory. Burstable means at least one container sets a request but not equal-limits for all resources. BestEffort means no requests or limits at all. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts in the order BestEffort first, then Burstable that exceed their requests, and Guaranteed last, and the OOM killer uses a correlated oom_score so BestEffort processes are killed before Guaranteed ones. An emptyDir volume shares the Pod's lifecycle, so its data is created when the Pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the Pod is removed or rescheduled, which is why its contents do not survive a reschedule.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, when the branch runs short of space, management decides who gets moved out first. BestEffort tellers made no reservation, so they are moved first. Burstable tellers reserved a small desk but spread onto extra space, so they are moved next if they overflowed their reservation. Guaranteed tellers reserved exactly the space they use, so they are protected and moved last. An emptyDir is a scratch notepad clipped to the teller's badge; the moment that teller leaves the building the notepad is thrown away, so nothing written on it survives their departure.

**One line to remember:** Guaranteed Pods survive longest and BestEffort die first under memory pressure, and emptyDir is scratch space tied to the Pod, so it vanishes on restart or reschedule.

sections.s2_technical:
The QoS class is derived, not set directly. If every container in the Pod specifies both a memory request and limit and both a CPU request and limit, and the requests equal the limits, the Pod is Guaranteed. If the Pod has at least one request or limit set but does not meet the strict equality for all containers and resources, it is Burstable. If no container sets any request or limit, it is BestEffort. You can see the class with `kubectl get pod -o jsonpath` on the status QoS field or in `kubectl describe pod`.

The class drives eviction under node memory pressure. When a node runs low on allocatable memory, the kubelet begins evicting Pods to reclaim it, and it ranks candidates so BestEffort Pods go first because they reserved nothing, then Burstable Pods that are using more than their requests, and Guaranteed Pods last. Separately, the Linux OOM killer assigns each process an oom_score_adj that Kubernetes sets according to QoS, so if the kernel itself has to kill a process, a BestEffort container has a much higher kill priority than a Guaranteed one. The practical lesson for banking is to make critical services Guaranteed by setting requests equal to limits, so a noisy BestEffort batch job cannot cause the kubelet to evict the Transfer Service first.

A subtlety is that CPU and memory behave differently. CPU is compressible, so exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container rather than killing it. Memory is incompressible, so exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled, and under node pressure the QoS ranking decides who is evicted. That is why memory requests and limits deserve the most care.

The emptyDir question is about lifecycle. An emptyDir volume is created empty when the Pod is scheduled to a node and lives on that node's disk, or in memory if the medium is memory. Its lifetime is exactly the Pod's lifetime on that node. If a container in the Pod restarts, the emptyDir survives because the Pod is still the same Pod on the same node. But if the Pod itself is deleted, evicted, or rescheduled to a different node, the emptyDir and everything in it are gone, because the Pod it belonged to no longer exists and a brand-new Pod gets a brand-new empty emptyDir. This is why emptyDir is correct for scratch data like a cache, a temporary download, or a scratch space shared between containers in the same Pod, but completely wrong for anything that must persist. For durable data in a bank, such as a ledger or uploaded documents, I use a PersistentVolumeClaim backed by a PersistentVolume, whose lifecycle is independent of any Pod, so the data survives Pod restarts, reschedules, and even node loss. The senior discipline is to match the volume type to the durability requirement: emptyDir for ephemeral scratch, PersistentVolumeClaim for durable state, and a StatefulSet with per-replica claims for stateful workloads.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India two incidents taught us about QoS and emptyDir.

Problem 1 — a BestEffort nightly report job with no limits ballooned in memory and caused node pressure, and the kubelet evicted our Transfer Service first because the Transfer Service was Burstable at the time. We made the Transfer Service Guaranteed so it would be protected. This is exactly the eviction-order lesson.

Problem 2 — a developer cached generated account statements in an emptyDir to speed up re-downloads. When the Pod rescheduled to another node during a deploy, every cached statement vanished and users re-generated them, which was fine for a cache but would have been catastrophic if that data had been the only copy. This is exactly the emptyDir lifecycle lesson, and it is why the authoritative statements live in a PersistentVolume.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `QosClassifier` that derives the QoS class from requests and limits, a `NodeMemoryPressure` evictor that ranks Pods and evicts in QoS order, and a `VolumeLifecycle` model contrasting emptyDir (lost on reschedule) with a PersistentVolumeClaim (survives). We protect the Transfer Service serving Rajesh and Priya and show the statement cache loss.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the QoS + volume simulation
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/qos/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.qos.QosDemo

# Real cluster: inspect QoS class and eviction behaviour
kubectl get pod transfer-xyz -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'   # Guaranteed
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -i evict                    # eviction events
kubectl get pvc ledger-pvc                                      # durable claim bound
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three Pods with different resource settings and a statement cache written to both an emptyDir and a PVC.

Step 1 — The classifier derives each Pod's QoS. The nightly report sets nothing, so it is BestEffort. The statement cache sets requests below limits, so it is Burstable, and it is using 480 MiB against a 256 MiB request, so it is over its request. The Transfer Service sets requests equal to limits, so it is Guaranteed.

Step 2 — The node hits memory pressure and must evict one Pod. The evictor ranks candidates: BestEffort highest, then Burstable over its request, then Guaranteed lowest. The nightly report is BestEffort and ranks highest, so it is evicted first and the Transfer Service is protected.

Step 3 — Because the Transfer Service survived, a transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs successfully on the Guaranteed Pod. This is exactly why we made the critical service Guaranteed.

Step 4 — A generated statement for Rajesh is written to both the emptyDir cache and the PVC. Before any reschedule, both show the file.

Step 5 — The Pod is rescheduled to another node during a deploy. The emptyDir is deleted with the old Pod, so its contents are empty on the new Pod, while the PVC re-attaches and keeps the statement. This proves emptyDir is ephemeral and the PVC is durable.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Node under memory pressure
    │ rank by QoS
    ▼
  BestEffort (nightly-report)  ── evicted FIRST ──→ reclaimed
  Burstable over-request (cache) ── evicted next ──→
  Guaranteed (transfer-service) ── evicted LAST ──→ PROTECTED
    │
    ▼ transfer SAV2001→CUR3001 Rs.50000 (on surviving Guaranteed pod)

  Volume lifecycle:
  write statement → emptyDir[/tmp/cache]  +  PVC[/data/ledger]
    │ pod rescheduled to new node
    ▼
  emptyDir → []  (gone with old Pod)
  PVC      → [statement]  (re-attached, independent lifecycle)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kubernetes assigns each Pod a Quality of Service class that it derives from the resource requests and limits rather than from anything you set directly. A Pod is Guaranteed when every container sets both memory and CPU requests equal to their limits. It is Burstable when it sets some requests or limits but does not meet that strict equality across all containers and resources. It is BestEffort when it sets no requests or limits at all. I can read the derived class from the Pod's status.

That class directly controls who survives when a node runs short of memory. The kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods first because they reserved nothing, then Burstable Pods that are using more than their requests, and Guaranteed Pods last, and the Linux out-of-memory killer uses a correlated score so BestEffort processes are killed before Guaranteed ones. A key detail is that CPU is compressible, so exceeding a CPU limit only throttles the container, while memory is incompressible, so exceeding a memory limit gets the container killed outright, which is why memory requests and limits deserve the most care. The practical lesson for a bank is to make the critical path Guaranteed by setting requests equal to limits, so a noisy BestEffort batch job can never cause the kubelet to evict the payment service first.

The emptyDir behaviour comes down to lifecycle. An emptyDir volume is created empty when the Pod is scheduled to a node and it lives exactly as long as that Pod lives on that node. A container restart keeps the emptyDir because the Pod is still the same Pod, but if the Pod is deleted, evicted, or rescheduled to another node, the emptyDir and everything in it are gone, because a brand-new Pod gets a brand-new empty volume. That makes emptyDir perfect for scratch data like a cache or a temporary download and completely wrong for anything that must persist. For durable data I use a PersistentVolumeClaim whose lifecycle is independent of any Pod, so it survives restarts, reschedules, and even node loss.

In my project at the National Bank of India both ideas showed up in real incidents. A BestEffort nightly report job ballooned and caused node pressure, and the kubelet evicted our Transfer Service first because it was only Burstable at the time, so we made the Transfer Service Guaranteed and it has been protected ever since. Separately, a developer cached generated account statements in an emptyDir, and when the Pod rescheduled during a deploy every cached statement vanished, which was harmless for a cache but reinforced the rule that the authoritative statements must live in a PersistentVolume. Matching the QoS class to the service's importance and the volume type to the durability requirement is the discipline I carry from that.
